subject: Canadians sold a record $31B of U.S. stocks in July
bodyMarkdown:
If you own a target date fund or a couch potato portfolio inside your RRSP, you hold a slab of American tech whether you picked it or not. Canadians as a group sold more of that exposure in July than in any month on record, and the numbers landed on Thursday.

## What Statistics Canada actually counted

Statistics Canada published July's **portfolio flows** on Thursday, the tally of money crossing the border to buy and sell stocks and bonds rather than to build factories. Canadians sold a net $31.0 billion of US stocks and investment fund shares in the month (Canadian dollars, as the agency reports them), and Statistics Canada said the selling was concentrated in large cap US technology names. The Globe and Mail reported Thursday that this was the largest monthly net exodus from American markets on record, bigger than March 2020, when lockdowns crashed the market. The reversal is what got my attention. Over the first six months of 2026, Canadians bought a combined $78.1 billion of US equities, so July gave back a good chunk of half a year's buying in four weeks. It was not only stocks. Canadians also shed $5.1 billion of US government bonds, a sixth straight monthly reduction that takes the year's divestment there to $37.3 billion.

## Money moved the other way at the same time

While Canadians were selling America, international investors bought $20.7 billion of Canadian securities in July, mostly federal government bonds, which brings their total since January to $178.9 billion. They also picked up $7.2 billion of Canadian equities, which Statistics Canada called their largest monthly investment in Canadian shares so far this year. Selling of money market instruments took some of that back, and the month still netted out to a $51.3 billion inflow, against a $30.6 billion cut in what Canadians hold abroad. Two different bets are running here. Canadians stepped away from expensive US tech, and foreigners bought Canadian government debt at a moment when the Bank of Canada's overnight rate sits at 2.25% and the Fed's target range is 3.75% to 4%. Paying up for the lower yielding bond usually says something about the currency, or about wanting safety. I want two more months of data before I call it.

## My read on why

I do not think this was one bad week of nerves. The Globe and Mail, citing a Sun Life report, wrote that Canadians pulled money out of US equity funds in the first quarter at the fastest rate since the start of the pandemic and moved it into more conservative holdings, so the retreat was already underway well before July. Statistics Canada also noted that the price of the S&P 500 edged down during the month, which takes some of the drama out of a record. The nerves around AI names are real and recent: on September 14, after senior US executives called for slowing AI development, the S&P 500 fell 0.59% to 7,611.44 and Nvidia closed down 3.36%. A record month of Canadian selling, most of it in big tech, reads to me like rebalancing by people who got uncomfortable with one crowded trade.

## The takeaway

Watch two dates. The August flow numbers arrive from Statistics Canada in mid-October on its usual monthly schedule, and they will show whether July was a single month's reversal or the start of something longer. The Bank of Canada decides on October 28, a meeting CP24 reported on Thursday that markets now see as close to a coin flip between a hold and a hike, after September's hold at 2.25%. Before either, open your own statement and work out what share of your equity money sits in US large cap tech, because that is the position the country was trimming, and remember that flow data gets revised.
